---
title: "Gradients of Vector-Valued Functions"
description: "An original worked mathematical lesson corresponding to MML §5.3."
---

**Reference:** *Mathematics for Machine Learning*, Chapter 5, §5.3. The teaching example and explanation here are original.

## Why we need this concept

A batch model maps three parameters to six predictions, not to one scalar. Its derivative is therefore a Jacobian matrix.

## Derive the structure

$$
f:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R^{6},\qquad J_f(\boldsymbol\beta)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=X
$$

Check the shapes and conditions in this statement before applying it. The formula encodes the exact relationship to reason about, rather than replacing a derivation with a library call.

## Worked example

For f(beta)=X beta, changing beta by delta changes every prediction by X delta. The first two rows of X are (1,1,1) and (1,2,2); the first two output changes are respectively delta0+delta1+delta2 and delta0+2delta1+2delta2.

## Interpretation and limitations

A Jacobian propagates local changes from inputs to outputs. The gradient of a scalar-valued function can be viewed as a vector or as a row Jacobian depending on convention; state your orientation.

## Challenge

What dimensions must the Jacobian have for a map R^3 to R^6?
